claims.text: HTTP is stateless: each request is meant to be understood on its own, and a server is not required to relate two requests to each other.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 Abstract and §3 (HTTP is a stateless application-level protocol)

claims.text: Reuse of the underlying connection is a transport arrangement and does not by itself identify the sender of two requests.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §3.3 Connections and §9.3 (connection management is independent of message semantics)

claims.text: A server sends a cookie to a client with a Set-Cookie header in a response; the client returns stored cookies to that server with a Cookie header in later requests.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §4.1 Set-Cookie and §4.2 Cookie

claims.text: One Set-Cookie header carries one cookie; the Cookie request header may carry several name-value pairs on one line.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §4.1.1 (one cookie per Set-Cookie) and §4.2.1 (cookie-string, pairs separated by '; ')

claims.text: The client attaches the Cookie header on its own, without the request being written differently; it sends the stored cookies whose domain (the request's host name), path and Secure conditions the request matches, and a user agent is allowed to omit the header entirely.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §5.4 The Cookie Header (user agent computes cookie-list and includes it)

claims.text: The Path attribute limits which paths of the site a cookie is sent for; Path=/ therefore sends it on every path of that site.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §4.1.2.4 The Path Attribute and §5.1.4 Paths and Path-Match

claims.text: The HttpOnly attribute tells the client to withhold the cookie from non-HTTP interfaces, which is what keeps scripts running in the page from reading its value.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §4.1.2.6 The HttpOnly Attribute and §8.5

claims.text: The Secure attribute tells the client to send the cookie only over a connection it considers secure; HttpOnly does not encrypt anything, so without Secure and TLS the value travels readable.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §4.1.2.5 The Secure Attribute and §8.3 Clear Text

claims.text: The SameSite attribute restricts whether a cookie is sent on requests started by another site; SameSite=Lax is the restricted setting used by the lab.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265bis §5.2 The SameSite Attribute (not in RFC 6265; see open_questions)

claims.text: A cookie value such as sid=dev-session-1 is an identifier with no meaning outside the server that issued it; the state it stands for is held by that server, so the value is worth what that state is worth.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §1 (cookies used to maintain session state) and §8.2 Ambient Authority

claims.text: At tag stage-0 the lab answers /login.html with the header Set-Cookie: sid=dev-session-1; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax, and the site is served over plain HTTP on port 8080, so no Secure attribute is set.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0, handle /login.html; outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cookie-roundtrip.txt step 2

claims.text: At tag stage-0 /admin answers 401 with no Cookie header, 200 when the Cookie line contains sid=, and 403 when it contains role=guest; both tests are substring matches on the header, so the lab keeps no state behind the value.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0, handle /admin route with @guest and @signedIn matchers; outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cookie-roundtrip.txt

claims.text: curl sends a request and prints the reply and keeps no cookies between runs unless told to: -c <file> saves what the server sets, -b <file> sends it back, -w '%{http_code}' prints the status code alone, -D - prints response headers, -sS hides progress, -o /dev/null discards the body.
claims.source_hint: curl manual, options --cookie-jar (-c), --cookie (-b), --write-out (-w), --dump-header (-D), --silent --show-error (-sS), --output (-o)

claims.text: In curl, -H 'Cookie: role=guest' writes the request header by hand, which is how step 5 of the script sends a cookie the server never set.
claims.source_hint: curl manual, option --header (-H)

claims.text: 401 is the answer when the request carries nothing the server accepts as identity. 403 says the server understood the request and refuses it; in this lab that happens for any Cookie line containing role=guest, while a Cookie line containing neither role=guest nor sid= answers 401.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.2 401 Unauthorized and §15.5.4 403 Forbidden

claims.text: The step 3 line of outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cookie-roundtrip.txt is the client's own record of what it stored: a host and a path, some flags curl writes, then the name sid and the value dev-session-1, and no personal data.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cookie-roundtrip.txt line 8; curl manual, cookie file format

claims.text: Because the client sends a stored cookie by itself on the requests its attributes allow, the attributes on Set-Cookie, and not the application code writing the request, decide who may read the value and when it travels.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6265 §8 Security Considerations

claims.text: www/login.html at stage-0 contains no form and no password field; opening it is enough to receive the cookie, because the header comes from the server configuration and not from the page.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang www/login.html and Caddyfile at stage-0 (header Set-Cookie then file_server)

claims.text: grep prints only the input lines matching its pattern, so step 2 prints the Set-Cookie line alone out of the response headers; tr '\t' ' ' in step 3 replaces tabs with spaces in the stored record.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 Shell and Utilities: grep, tr; outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/cookie-roundtrip.txt lines 5 and 8

claims.text: The name localhost in the script's addresses refers to the machine the script runs on, so the requests reach the lab started there.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6761 §6.3 (the 'localhost' special-use domain name)

beyond_scope: Section 5 explains curl's options and the filters grep and tr, and says what localhost names, because the script's five steps cannot be read without them; they are tool syntax, not cookie behaviour.
Section 5 names the Path attribute, which the outline does not list, because it appears in the header the lab actually sets and would otherwise be an unexplained word in a quoted line.
Sections 3 and 5 use 'stateless', 'session identifier' and 'attribute' as plain words; none is a glossary term, and outline items 1 and 4 cannot be stated without them.

open_questions: Owner only — content/versions.yaml has no key whose docs root covers cookies: the http key points at RFC 9110, which does not define Set-Cookie. Claims 3-10 name RFC 6265, downloaded to refs/rfc/ per DECISIONS D9 but not admissible as an official docs root today. A key such as http_cookies pointing at RFC 6265 would let reviewer 04 verify them.

Owner only — claim 9 (SameSite) has no source in RFC 6265 at all; the attribute is defined in RFC 6265bis, which is not in refs/rfc/. The lesson states SameSite only at the level of what it restricts, so an unverified verdict on a behaviour claim does not block approval, but the reviewer cannot confirm it from the evidence on disk.

Owner only — review 04 minor (section 5): the lab answers /admin with 401 from a bare Caddy respond, without the WWW-Authenticate header RFC 9110 §15.5.2 requires, so the run this lesson reads is one no conforming server may send. The reviewer's fix is a depth_notes line on this lesson in content/tracks/foundation/track.yaml ('401 của lab dùng cookie nên không kèm WWW-Authenticate; không dạy khung xác thực HTTP ở đây'), which is an outline change and needs the owner. The lesson text is left alone, as the reviewer asked.
